title: CI/CD for GTM: Continuous Deployment for Go-to-Market
summary: CI/CD for GTM means every change to enrichment, scoring, routing and sequences ships as a pull request that is planned, checked, approved, deployed on merge, logged and reversible. What each software CI/CD step becomes for go-to-market, and how to set it up on Cargo.
body_markdown:
**CI/CD for go-to-market (GTM CI/CD) means every change to how you enrich, score, route and reach leads ships the way software ships: as a pull request that shows what will change and what it will send and spend, passes a check, gets approved, deploys automatically when it merges, is logged, and can be reverted. On Cargo, you declare the go-to-market engine as a TypeScript project in a git repository and connect that repository in Settings → States. From then on Cargo comments a plan on every pull request and holds large merges until a reviewer adds the` cargo:approve-impact` label. Every merge to the production branch runs` cargo-ai project deploy --yes` as a service user.**


## Why go-to-market needs it#


In most go-to-market stacks a change goes live the moment someone clicks save. A new lead score threshold, a routing rule, an extra enrichment step or a sequence edit takes effect on the next record, with nobody reviewing it first. Nothing tells you beforehand how many contacts the edit will email or how many credits it will burn, and undoing it depends on someone remembering what the old setting was.


Software teams solved the same problem decades ago. Code changes go through a pull request, an automated build checks them, a reviewer approves them, a pipeline deploys them, and every deploy is recorded so a bad one can be reverted.[Building go-to-market now looks like building software](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/building-gtm-looks-like-building-software) , and the same discipline applies once the engine lives in files.


## Each CI/CD step, for go-to-market#


Software CI/CD step Go-to-market equivalent On Cargo


Source control Models, plays, tools and agents live in a repository` cargo-ai project init` , or` cargo-ai project pull` to generate code from an existing workspace


Build The project must compile before anything ships` cargo-ai project check` , offline; the **Cargo** check fails when the project does not compile


Diff See which live resources a change touches` cargo-ai project plan` , and the same plan as a comment on every pull request


Impact report See what the merge will send and spend The “On merge” table: records, emails, LinkedIn actions, messages and credits, per play and batch


Approval A named person signs off on large changes Above set limits, the check waits until someone adds the` cargo:approve-impact` label


Deploy Merging is the release Every push to the production branch runs` cargo-ai project deploy --yes` as a service user


Deploy log Who shipped what, and whether it worked Every plan and deploy is listed on the project’s state in Settings → States, with its status


Rollback Undo a bad release` git revert` , then merge the revert


Tests Try the change on something small first A pilot batch on 50 records, a play shipped with` isEnabled: false` , and agent evals


The rest of this page walks through setting it up and shipping one change.


## Set it up#


Put the project in git and push it to GitHub:


shellscript


```text
npm   install   -g   @cargo-ai/cli
cargo-ai   login   --email   you@company.com
cargo-ai   project   init   acme-gtm        # scaffolds the project and creates its deploy state
cd   acme-gtm   &&   git   push


```


Then connect the repository:


1. **Settings → Connectors → GitHub** : connect your GitHub account and install the Cargo GitHub app on the repository.
2. **Settings → States** : open the project’s state and pick the repository, the production branch and the directory that holds` cargo.state.json` . From a terminal,` cargo-ai project state connect` does the same for an existing project.
3. **In GitHub branch protection** , make the **Cargo** check required on the production branch, so a failed or waiting check actually blocks the merge.


There is no workflow file to write and no Cargo API token to store in GitHub. The[GitHub page](https://www.getcargo.ai/github) covers what the app does, and[deploy go-to-market changes on merge](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/deploy-go-to-market-changes-on-merge) covers every option of the connection.


## One change, start to finish#


Take a play that enriches, scores and routes every new HubSpot contact:


typescript


```text
// infra/plays/inbound.ts
import   { definePlay }   from   "@cargo-ai/cdk"  ;


import   { contacts }   from   "../models/contacts"  ;
import   { enrichScoreAndRoute }   from   "../workflows/enrichScoreAndRoute"  ;


export   const   inbound   =   definePlay  (  "inbound"  , {
model: contacts,   // HubSpot contacts, synced by a connector-backed model
changeKinds: [  "added"  ],
schedule: { type:   "realtime"   },
workflow: enrichScoreAndRoute,
});


```


Someone on the team wants to post a Slack message to the account owner whenever a contact scores above the routing threshold. They add the step to` enrichScoreAndRoute` on a branch and open a pull request.


**The plan.** Cargo clones the commit into a sandbox, compiles it with your pinned` @cargo-ai/cdk` , and diffs it against the deploy state. The comment lists` play:inbound` as an update and leaves the other resources counted as unchanged. A plan never gets a Cargo credential, so opening a pull request changes nothing in the workspace.


**The impact.** Above the resource table, the “On merge” table counts the records the play runs on and the chat messages its steps can send for them, as upper bounds. That is the part a resource diff cannot tell you:[preview what a change will send](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/preview-go-to-market-changes-before-merge) explains how each column is counted.


**The approval.** If the totals across the pull request go above 100 emails, 100 LinkedIn actions, 100 chat messages, 5,000 audience adds or 2,500 credits, the check shows **Action required** with the title **Needs approval: add the cargo:approve-impact label** . A reviewer reads the table and adds the label, Cargo plans again, and the check passes.[Require approval before a high-impact change goes live](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/require-approval-for-high-impact-go-to-market-changes) covers who should hold that label.


**The deploy.** Merging pushes to the production branch, and Cargo runs` cargo-ai project deploy --yes` on that commit as the connection’s service user, with a credential minted for the run and revoked when it ends. Deploys of one project run one at a time, in order. While Deploy on push is on, Cargo refuses a deploy from anyone else, so the merge is the only way the change reaches production.


**The log.** The deploy appears on the project’s state in Settings → States as queued, running, success, error or cancelled, recorded with the commit it ran on. Git keeps the diff and the review, and the pull request’s timeline shows who added the approval label.


**The undo.** If routing goes wrong,` git revert <sha>` on a branch, open the pull request, and merge it. The plan shows the diff going back, and the deploy reconciles the workspace to the previous definitions.[Roll back a go-to-market change](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/roll-back-a-go-to-market-change) covers stopping a play first and what a revert cannot recall.


## Testing before production#


Continuous integration is more than a diff. For go-to-market, the most useful test is a pilot on a few records before a play runs on all of them. A dry run shows an action’s output and price before you wire it in, and an eval suite checks each agent’s prompt.[Test a go-to-market change before it reaches production](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/test-a-go-to-market-change-before-production) walks through each one, and[evaluate an agent before production](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/evaluate-go-to-market-agents-before-production) covers agent prompts in depth.


## Limits worth knowing#


- **Messages already sent stay sent.** A revert stops future enrollments. Emails, LinkedIn actions and records written to your CRM are not recalled, which is why the preview and the approval come before the merge.
- **Edits in the Cargo UI bypass the pipeline.** Resources deployed from code stay editable in the app, and the project never reads those edits back. Pick one owner per resource, and run` cargo-ai project refresh` to see what drifted.
- **Pull requests from forks are not planned.**
- **Anyone who can push to the production branch can deploy.** Protect that branch the way you protect production.


Prefer your own CI? The connected repository runs the same two commands,` cargo-ai project plan` and` cargo-ai project deploy` , that your pipeline can run. To have a coding agent make the change for you on the pull request, see[ask @cargo on a pull request](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/ask-cargo-on-a-pull-request) . The full lifecycle, one page per step, is in[GTM as code: the complete guide](https://www.getcargo.ai/blog/gtm-as-code-complete-guide) .


## FAQ#


CI/CD for GTM (go-to-market) applies continuous integration and continuous deployment to the systems that enrich, score, route and reach leads and accounts. Every change is a pull request that is planned, checked and approved before it merges, deployed automatically on merge, recorded, and reversible with a git revert.


No. Once the repository is connected in Settings → States, Cargo plans every pull request and deploys every merge to the production branch itself, with no workflow file and no Cargo token stored in GitHub. Teams that prefer their own CI can run cargo-ai project plan and cargo-ai project deploy from it instead.


A comment with the resources that change, and an “On merge” table that counts, for each play and one-off batch or run, the records it runs on, the emails, LinkedIn actions and messages it can send, and the credits it can spend.


Revert the commit in git and merge the revert’s pull request. The deploy reconciles the workspace to whatever the code says. Messages already sent and records already written are not recalled.
